vignette:
Mariana, a 39-year-old non-profit worker living in a midsized city with her husband, went to bed one Tuesday night in late autumn feeling content-she had just finished organizing a community health fair and was proud of the work. She woke a few hours later to a glint of metal in the moonlight. A man stood over her holding a knife from her own kitchen. He forced her out of bed, made her remove her clothes, and then assaulted her while pressing the blade against her throat. She remembers fragments: the cold floor tiles, the sound of his breathing, the way the knife caught the light. But she cannot put those fragments in the right order. When she tries to tell her therapist what happened, the words dissolve. What comes instead is a wave of rage so hot it feels like it will burn through her chest. She often thinks that someone else-someone stronger, someone less naive-would never have ended up in that situation, would have locked the door or fought back or screamed.

In the months afterward, Mariana's life contracted. She used to feel safe in her own home, especially at night; now dusk is the worst time, and she finds herself checking the locks three, four times before she can sit still. Her husband tells her she is safe now, that the man is in prison, and she knows he means it, but the words do not land. She cannot believe safety exists anywhere. Any unexpected sound-a car backfiring, a dropped pan-makes her jump out of her skin. She stopped cooking with knives; her husband prepares all meals. When she showers, she leaves the bathroom door open because being naked, even in her own locked house, fills her with a dread she cannot explain.

Mariana's job at a nonprofit community center once anchored her identity. She ran evening programs for new immigrant families, many of them Latin American like her. Now she has stopped taking evening shifts. She tells her supervisor she needs daylight hours, but the real reason is that the walk from the bus stop after sunset triggers a vigilance she cannot control. She also stopped attending the center's cultural potlucks, where she used to feel a deep connection to her heritage. That loss-of community, of the rituals that made her feel like herself-is something she grieves almost daily. She has come to believe she is a weak person, someone who fell apart when she should have held together. The belief colors everything: how she interacts with her husband (she pulls away, sure he must see her as pathetic), how she responds to colleagues' invitations, how she looks at herself in the mirror.

Her husband finally persuaded her to call a clinic after she spent an entire Saturday curled on the bathroom floor, sobbing with rage about something she could not articulate. The rage scares her most of all-it flares without warning, aimed at no one and at everyone, and it feels as present now as it did the morning after the assault. She is afraid she will never feel like the same person, the person who used to laugh easily and walk through the world without flinching. But she is also afraid, she admits quietly, that the therapy might not work, that she will stay stuck in this fog of vigilance and fury and self-blame. She wants to find her way back to her community, to the evenings she once loved, to a body that does not feel like a trap. She just does not know how to begin.
